basics.name: Cian McCaul
basics.label: Computer Science student at DCU
basics.headline: I build software that runs real businesses.
basics.summary: I built the booking, payments and staff platform that **BodyMed Healthcare**, a clinic in Clontarf, runs on. Patients book and pay online, and staff run the clinic from one hub.
bio: I’m Cian and I live in Dublin. I spent my early years in Fall River, Nova Scotia, before my family moved to Clontarf in 2015. Starting again in a new country taught me to adapt quickly, and I still like being thrown into something new.

What I enjoy most is building things that make people’s day easier. At BodyMed Healthcare I’ve gone from admin work to building the booking, payments and staff platform the clinic runs on, working with the owner, reception and the therapists. Their feedback changed what I built, and taught me that the people who use a system every day know the job better than I do.

On Saturday mornings I coach at Rugbytots, where I went from assistant coach to head coach, running four classes for young children. My favourite moment is a child finally scoring their first conversion.

Next, I want to keep building software that real people rely on, and to do it in a team of experienced engineers, where I can learn faster than I could on my own. That’s why I’m looking for a software engineering internship.

projects.name: Clinic platform
projects.tagline: Online booking, payments and a staff hub for a real clinic.
projects.description: The clinic already took bookings online through Jane, but nobody paid until the end of the appointment. Late cancellations and no-shows cost therapists money, and reception tracked payments by hand. I replaced it with one system on top of the clinic’s diary (Cliniko) and payments (Stripe): patients pay when they book, reception handles refunds, fees and phone bookings from one dashboard, and each therapist is paid straight into their own Stripe account.

outcome.text: In its first 10 days, appointments paid in advance rose from 0% to 14.5%.

projects.fact: Live at book.bodymed.ie since 30 October 2026, taking real bookings and payments every day.

highlights.text: Built a pay-at-booking system on Cliniko and Stripe for a physiotherapy clinic; in its first 10 days, appointments paid in advance rose from 0% to 14.5%.
highlights.fallback: Built a pay-at-booking system on Cliniko and Stripe for a physiotherapy clinic, live since 30 October 2026.

highlights.text: Moved 90% of the clinic’s new online bookings onto the new system within 10 days of launch, with no drop in online booking volume.

highlights: Designed a pay-then-book flow with slot holds, idempotent webhooks and automatic refunds, so a patient is never left paid but not booked, or booked twice.
Wrote a failure-mode analysis, test plan, runbook and decision records before launch; 142 tests pass.

projects.name: AI email triage
projects.tagline: A prototype that sorts a clinic inbox, drafts replies and learns from staff edits.
projects.description: A working prototype, tested on sample emails. It sorts clinic email by topic and urgency, drafts replies and learns from the changes staff make before they press send. Built-in rules do the sorting in the public demo; with a Groq key, an AI model (Llama 3.3) sorts and drafts replies from the clinic’s handbook instead. A red-flag check runs on every email, whichever sorter is used.
projects.outcome: The built-in rule-based sorter put all 12 labelled test emails in the right folder on repeated runs, including every urgent-symptom email and the cases built to trick a keyword filter.
projects.fact: 37 tests, including one that checks every sample email lands in its expected folder.
highlights: Built a prototype that sorts clinic email into four folders, drafts replies and learns from staff edits.
Its rule-based sorter filed all 12 labelled test emails correctly on repeated runs, with a red-flag check and 37 tests.
projects.imageAlt: An email in the triage demo titled Pins and needles getting worse. One panel explains why it was sorted into Priority, and a safety check says the draft reply tells the patient to contact their GP or emergency department first.

projects.name: Clinic chatbot
projects.tagline: Answers common questions and points patients to the right physio.
projects.description: A chat widget for a physio clinic. It answers common questions, suggests the right physio for back, knee, shoulder or sports injuries, and hands anything else to staff. The replies are plain rules, not AI, so the clinic decides exactly what patients are told.
projects.fact: Rule-based on purpose: every answer is predictable, so nothing goes off-script on health advice.
projects.imageAlt: The chatbot demo on a fictional clinic’s site. Asked about a back injury, it suggests a physiotherapist and offers a link to book.
projects.outcome: Urgent symptoms, such as chest pain, trouble breathing or signs of a stroke, get a “call 112 or 999, or your GP” message, checked before every other rule. 35 tests.

projects.name: Jarvis site monitor
projects.tagline: Explains outages in plain English and proposes guarded fixes.
projects.description: Checks the sites I look after every 15 minutes. When one goes down it explains the outage in plain English with AI and, if the fix is small and safe, opens a pull request I can approve from my phone.
projects.outcome: In deliberate test outages on a sandbox site, Jarvis caught and explained both failures and opened one-line fix pull requests, which I merged after review.
projects.fact: Every AI-proposed fix passes five guard rails enforced in code, not in a prompt.
highlights: Built a monitor that checks sites every 15 minutes, explains outages with an LLM and opens small fix pull requests.
Enforced five guard rails in code: pull request only, one file, 15 changed lines or fewer, scoped token, fail closed.

guardRails.title: Never touches main
guardRails.detail: It only ever opens a pull request.

guardRails.title: One file only
guardRails.detail: A fix that touches more is rejected.

guardRails.title: 15 changed lines or fewer
guardRails.detail: Anything bigger is flagged for manual review.

guardRails.title: Scoped token
guardRails.detail: Access to the monitored sites’ repos only. It can’t modify itself.

guardRails.title: Fails closed
guardRails.detail: If anything is ambiguous, no pull request is opened and the reason is recorded.

projects.imageAlt: The Jarvis dashboard in dark blue. A list of incidents for the monitored sites, and an Ask Jarvis panel explaining a 500 error in plain English, with buttons to review the pull request on GitHub or approve and merge it.
projects.imageCaption: The Jarvis dashboard: incidents, a plain-English diagnosis, and one-tap approve & merge.
